logos.summary: John opens his Gospel by calling the Son of God the Logos, the Word. The Word was with God and was God, and became flesh. The Fathers read this to mean the Son is eternal and not made. He is the one through whom God made the world and speaks to it. The Catechism builds the teaching of the Incarnation on it.

steps.0: Logos can mean a spoken word, an account, or reason. John uses it as a name for a divine Person.
steps.1: The eternal Word enters history as a human being.
steps.2: Hebrews says God’s last word to us is a Son.
steps.3: Justin says Christ is the Logos, and that human reason shares in him.
steps.4: Augustine says the Word “was” in the beginning, so he did not come to be.
steps.5: Athanasius says only the one who made us can make us new.
steps.6: The Catechism puts “Word” among the apostles’ confessions of Christ as God.
steps.7: “Incarnation” is drawn from John’s phrase “the Word became flesh”.

objections: John and the Fathers used a word Greek readers knew. They gave it a meaning no philosopher had: a divine Person who becomes a man and dies. Justin treats the reasonable part of pagan thought as a seed.

Augustine meets this. Human words sound and pass. John says the Word was God and all things were made through him. So the Word cannot be a passing sound. Athanasius adds that the Son is not a creature.
Scripture rules this out. John says the Word became flesh and we saw his glory. Revelation names the one in the bloody robe “The Word of God”. A message cannot become flesh.

ekklesia.summary: Ekklesia means a people called together, an assembly. Jesus promises to build his ekklesia on Peter and gives it authority to bind and loose. The apostles use the word for local communities and for the whole body of believers. The Fathers say this assembly is one, visible, and the mother of Christians.

steps.0: The Greek word is ekklesia. This Bible says “assembly” where many say “church”.
steps.1: The ekklesia here is a real community that can hear a dispute and give a judgment.
steps.2: After Pentecost the word names the community of the baptized.
steps.3: Paul tells the elders of Ephesus to shepherd the assembly of the Lord.
steps.4: Paul takes the word beyond a local meeting. The ekklesia is the body of which Christ is head.
steps.5: Ignatius treats the local church as an ordered community around its bishop.
steps.6: Cyprian says the Church is the mother through whom Christians are born.
steps.7: The Catechism says the first Christians called themselves ekklesia, the called-together.
steps.8: The Church’s use keeps three meanings together: the assembly, the local community, and the whole Church.

objections: The New Testament shows a visible assembly with real shepherds. Paul says the Spirit made the elders of Ephesus overseers. He calls the assembly the pillar and ground of the truth.
In ordinary Greek it can mean any gathering. But Jesus joins it to “I will build”, to a promise that Hades will not win, and to binding and loosing. These do not fit a passing meeting.

mysterion-sacramentum.summary: Paul uses mysterion for God’s hidden plan, now shown in Christ. Latin translators used sacramentum, a word that already meant an oath. The Fathers joined the two senses. The Church uses “sacrament” for the visible sign through which Christ’s saving work reaches us.

steps.0: In Paul a mysterion is not a puzzle. It is a hidden plan of God now made known, and it is Christ.
steps.1: Paul calls the whole Christian faith a mystery.
steps.2: Paul sees in husband and wife a sign of Christ and the Church.
steps.3: Sacramentum was a soldier’s oath. Tertullian uses it for baptism promises.
steps.4: Augustine says water becomes a sacrament when the word of Christ comes to it.
steps.5: Augustine reads Paul’s “great mystery” as the great sacrament.
steps.6: The Roman Catechism says sacrament is the Latin word for the Greek mysterion.
steps.7: A sacrament is a visible sign that gives what it shows.
steps.8: The Catechism says the two words are one idea in two languages.

objections: The Church teaches that a sacrament does what it signs. Augustine’s “visible word” and the Catechism’s “efficacious signs of grace” say the sign carries the gift.
The Church does not treat the seven as rivals to the one mystery. Christ is the mystery of salvation. The sacraments are the signs by which his grace reaches his members.
Tertullian shows why: a soldier’s oath is a solemn promise, and baptism is that kind of promise. The Latin Fathers settled on this word.

metanoia.summary: Metanoia means a change of mind that turns a person toward God. Jesus begins his preaching by calling people to repent. The apostles tie it to baptism and to deeds that show it. The Fathers taught that the Church can receive the sorry and forgive sins. The Catechism calls conversion a lifelong task.

steps.0: The verb is built from “after/change” and “to think”.
steps.1: John says real change of mind shows in changed living.
steps.2: Peter links repentance to baptism and forgiveness.
steps.3: Paul separates sorrow that leads to repentance from worldly regret.
steps.4: Tertullian says repentance is judged by changed life.
steps.5: Cyprian defends receiving back those who denied the faith, if their repentance is real.
steps.6: Ambrose says the Lord gave the Church power to forgive.
steps.7: Trent describes sorrow, rejecting sin, and the resolve to do better.
steps.8: The Catechism puts repentance at the heart of the Gospel.
steps.9: The Catechism explains that the word asks for a turn of the whole life.

objections: The Greek root means a change of mind. But in the New Testament it is never only in the head. John asks for fruits worthy of repentance. So does Paul. The Catechism says conversion shows itself in deeds.
The Church does not claim to forgive in her own right. Christ gave the apostles a share in his authority after the resurrection. Ambrose says denying this power denies the power of loosing.
Baptism is the first conversion. The Catechism says the call goes on through life as a second, lifelong conversion. Paul writes to believers about repentance.

homoousios.summary: “Homoousios” means “of one being”. It was put in the Creed at Nicaea in 325 to say the Son is truly God and shares the Father’s own being. He is not a creature. The word is not in the Bible. The Church used it to protect what the Bible says. Constantinople I and Chalcedon kept it.

steps.0: The Gospel states the unity plainly: “I and the Father are one”.
steps.1: Hebrews calls the Son the exact expression of God’s being.
steps.2: Jesus calls God his own Father, and his hearers hear that as equality with God.
steps.3: Nicaea says the Son is begotten of the Father’s own being.
steps.4: The bishops asked what the key words meant and agreed on their meaning.
steps.5: Athanasius defends the same meaning: the Son is of the Father’s being.
steps.6: Constantinople I kept the word in the Creed we still pray at Mass.
steps.7: Chalcedon uses it twice: one with the Father, and one with us.
steps.8: The Catechism: “of one being” means the Son is one God with the Father.

objections: The Arians could accept every Bible phrase and still say the Son was made. So the council needed a word that left no room for that. The Catechism says the Church gave philosophy words a new meaning.
A few raised that objection. The council answered: the Son is of the Father, but not a part of him. The historian Socrates records both.
No. The Church uses “being” for what is one in God. She uses “Person” for the real difference between Father, Son and Spirit.

theotokos.summary: “Theotokos” means “God-bearer”. Ephesus affirmed it in 431 to say the child Mary bore is truly the Son of God, one Person, not two. The title is about who Jesus is. It is not about Mary’s origin and not about Mary being the source of his divinity.

steps.0: Elizabeth, by the Spirit, calls Mary the mother of her Lord.
steps.1: The angel says the child will be the Son of the Most High.
steps.2: Paul says God’s Son was born of a woman.
steps.3: Cyril says Mary is not the source of God’s divinity. The Person she bore is the Word.
steps.4: Cyril makes the title a test of faith in the Incarnation.
steps.5: Chalcedon repeats the title and adds “according to his manhood”.
steps.6: John of Damascus says the title protects the truth that the Son of God is truly man.
steps.7: The Catechism ties the title to Elizabeth’s greeting.
steps.8: The Catechism says the title is a statement about Christ: one subject, not two.

objections: That was Nestorius’ objection. Cyril answers it. The title does not say the Word’s nature began from Mary. A mother is mother of a person, not of a nature.
The title is Elizabeth’s “Lord” made exact. John of Damascus says denying it denies that the one born of her is God. It protects Christ.
No. Mary is a creature, a human mother. The title speaks of her Son. Her honour flows from that.

hesed.summary: Hesed is the Hebrew word for God’s faithful love. It is a love that ties itself to a people and keeps its word even when they fail. English Bibles say “loving kindness”, “steadfast love” or “mercy”. The Church hears in it the heart of God’s name and sees it fulfilled in Christ.

steps.0: After the golden calf, God tells his own name. Hesed is part of it.
steps.1: The psalm repeats hesed after every act of God.
steps.2: The prophet says God wants hesed from his people, a faithful heart and not only rituals.
steps.3: Augustine’s Latin Bible says “mercy”. He sees it as what is special in God’s works.
steps.4: Chrysostom takes “I will have mercy, and not sacrifice” and draws a plain lesson.
steps.5: The Catechism takes Exodus 34:6 as a summary of God’s name.
steps.6: The Church sees God’s hesed fully shown when the Father gives up his Son.

objections: The covenant is like a family bond, not a business deal. In Hosea, God’s faithfulness is like the love for a wandering partner. God says he wants mercy more than outward sacrifice.
The same sentence that names hesed says God does not ignore evil. His love is not carelessness. The Church holds that his mercy and his justice are both real.

eucharistia.summary: Eucharistia is the Greek word for thanksgiving. The Gospels use its verb when Jesus gives thanks over the bread at the Last Supper. The first Christians used it as the name of the sacrament. The Church still calls the Mass this way because it is a great act of thanks to the Father through Christ.

steps.0: The verb “gave thanks” is the root of the word. Jesus gave thanks over the bread.
steps.1: Paul passes on what he received. The thanksgiving is part of it.
steps.2: Paul says the blessing is a real sharing in Christ’s body and blood.
steps.3: Ignatius already uses “the Eucharist” as the settled name.
steps.4: Justin says Christians give thanks for creation and redemption.
steps.5: For Justin the thanksgiving is also the pure offering that Malachi foretold.
steps.6: The Catechism names the Greek verbs and the Jewish meal blessings behind them.
steps.7: The whole Eucharistic prayer is gratitude to the Father.

objections: The word names the prayer. But the prayer is said over the bread and cup that Jesus called his body and blood. Paul says eating unworthily makes one guilty of the body and blood.
The Gospels give the verb in the accounts of the Supper. By the early second century Ignatius and Justin use the noun as a fixed name. It grew from what Jesus did and said.

episkopos.summary: Episkopos means “overseer”, someone who watches over a flock. In the New Testament it stands next to “elder”. By the early second century it names the single pastor of each local Church. The Church sees the bishop as carrying on the apostles’ work of teaching and shepherding.

steps.0: Paul greets the Church at Philippi with its overseers and servants.
steps.1: Paul tells the elders of Ephesus the Spirit made them overseers.
steps.2: The office is called a good work, and the letter lists the character it needs.
steps.3: Titus is told to appoint elders. The same men are called overseers.
steps.4: About 107, Ignatius shows one bishop in each Church, with elders and deacons.
steps.5: Ignatius sees the bishop as the visible centre of unity.
steps.6: Chrysostom explains why Paul moves from bishops to deacons.
steps.7: The Catechism teaches that the apostles’ shepherding goes on in the order of bishops.

objections: At first the titles overlapped, as Titus and Chrysostom note. But the office with the apostles’ authority is already there. Ignatius shows one bishop at the head of each church within a generation.
The Catechism teaches that the apostles themselves named successors to carry on their work. The office carries the mission of teaching and shepherding.

pistis-faith.summary: Pistis means both trust and the thing believed. In Scripture, faith is the whole person’s answer to God who reveals himself. Abraham and Mary are its models. The Church teaches that faith is a gift of grace, a free human act, and the start of salvation.

steps.0: Paul calls his mission bringing about the obedience of faith.
steps.1: Hebrews gives the classic description: confidence in what God has promised, even if we cannot yet see it.
steps.2: Real faith is active in love.
steps.3: Augustine says trust comes first and opens the way to understanding.
steps.4: Augustine says faith is not just something we make. God begins it by grace.
steps.5: Trent says faith is the start of Christian life, which then grows.
steps.6: The Catechism: faith engages the whole person.
steps.7: Trust and belief are held together as one act.

objections: Paul and James speak of different things. Paul speaks against relying on works of the law. James speaks against a faith that never acts. Both say living faith works through love.
The Church holds both. Faith is only possible by grace, and it is still a real human act. The Catechism says believing is not against human freedom or reason.

parousia-and-eschaton.summary: Parousia is the Greek word for “coming” or “presence”. The New Testament uses it for Christ’s return in glory at the end of the age. The Fathers spoke of two comings, the first in humility and the second in glory. In the Creed the Church says he will come again to judge the living and the dead.

steps.0: Jesus uses the word for his return and warns that no one knows the day.
steps.1: Paul says the dead in Christ rise first and all are gathered.
steps.2: Angels link the Ascension to the return.
steps.3: Justin is an early witness to two comings.
steps.4: Hippolytus ties the second coming to the Antichrist and the end.
steps.5: Cyril teaches new Christians that the second coming is part of the preaching.
steps.6: Constantinople I puts it in the Creed we say at Mass.
steps.7: The Catechism ties it to the last judgment and the victory of good over evil.
steps.8: The return could happen at any moment, and no one can know when.

objections: Peter takes up this very question. Delay is patience, not failure. God wants everyone to have time to repent. The Catechism says the coming could happen at any moment.

The Church says no. The kingdom is fulfilled by God’s victory over evil at the end. It is not brought in by the Church or any human movement. The Catechism rejects even milder forms of an earthly kingdom.

kenosis-and-incarnation.summary: Kenosis comes from Philippians 2:7. The Son of God “emptied himself” by taking the form of a servant. The Fathers said this was not a loss of his divinity. It was adding a human nature. He became truly man and stayed truly God. The Church sees the Incarnation as God saving us from inside our own life.

steps.0: Paul’s hymn says the Son in the form of God emptied himself.
steps.1: John says the Word did not stop being the Word but became flesh.
steps.2: Athanasius says the Word took a body so that he could die for all.
steps.3: Athanasius: he became what we are, so we might share his life.
steps.4: Augustine reads kenosis as addition, not subtraction.
steps.5: Augustine says the emptying does not mean losing the form of God.
steps.6: Chalcedon receives a letter saying kenosis is compatible with the Son staying what he is.
steps.7: The Catechism quotes the Philippians hymn about the Incarnation.
steps.8: The Incarnation is the mark of true Christian faith.

objections: No. The Fathers and councils all say that kenosis is not a loss or change of divinity. The Catechism says he became truly man while remaining truly God.
Athanasius says it was fitting for the Word to take a mortal body, because only so could he die for all and renew us. What seems unworthy is the proof of his love.
